The backwards poster

For a school film, Milo painted a poster saying "Have you seen our bear?" It had a red ____1____ around its edge. The poster would appear in the opening shot.

When the camera image appeared on the classroom screen, the writing looked ____2____. Milo thought his lettering was wrong. He read the poster aloud. On the paper, the words were perfectly ____3____.

The tablet’s front camera preview showed a mirror image, the teacher explained. They checked a saved test clip rather than guessing from the ____4____. The recorded words were the right way round.

 He had almost ____5____ the whole poster to solve a problem that was only in the preview. His friend Jo held up a book with a printed title. In the preview, that title looked backwards too, giving them a simple ____6____.

They filmed the opening scene. Milo's character pinned up the poster and hurried away. Then a corner came loose and covered half the bear's face. They had to stop, but this time the trouble was ____7____, not an effect of the screen.

Jo added a stronger hidden clip. They checked that the clip would not fall into the walking route, then filmed ____8____. The poster stayed flat.

Later, the class watched the saved scene.  Two different problems had required two different ____9____. One had been solved by understanding the image; the other by ____10____ the poster.

Milo wrote "check the saved file" on their equipment list. Jo added "check the ____11____ too". The camera could show them a picture, but it could not ____12____ every loose corner. Before the next scene, they looked around the whole ____13____. This time, the delay was caused by the actor playing the missing bear: he had gone to get water without telling ____14____. Milo called him back. Some problems were easier to ____15____ than others.
